name: 1 Samuel
v: The Philistines pulled their forces together for war. They massed at Socoh in Judah and pitched camp between Socoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel rallied and camped in the Valley of Elah, lining up for battle against the Philistines.
The Philistines held one ridge, Israel held the other, with the valley gaping between them.
Out of the Philistine camp stepped a champion. His name was Goliath of Gath. He stood nearly ten feet tall.
A bronze helmet sat on his head, and he wore a coat of scaled bronze armor weighing one hundred twenty-five pounds.
Bronze guards on his legs, a bronze javelin slung across his back.
His spear shaft was thick as a weaver's beam, its iron head alone weighing fifteen pounds. A shield-bearer walked ahead of him.
He planted himself there and bellowed at the Israelite ranks: "Why have you all come out to line up for war? I am a Philistine. You are Saul's slaves. Pick a man. Send him down to me.
If he can fight me and kill me, we will be your servants. But if I take him down — if I kill him — you become ours. You will serve us."
The Philistine roared on: "I spit on the armies of Israel today! Give me a man — let's fight!"
Saul heard it. All Israel heard it. And they were shattered, terrified to the bone.
Now David was the son of an Ephrathite named Jesse from Bethlehem in Judah. Jesse had eight sons. By Saul's day, he was old, well along in years.
The three eldest had followed Saul to war — Eliab the firstborn, Abinadab next, then Shammah.
David was the youngest. The three oldest were with Saul,
but David shuttled back and forth from Saul's camp to Bethlehem, tending his father's sheep.
Morning and evening, for forty days straight, the Philistine strode out and took his stand.
One day Jesse said to David, "Take this sack of roasted grain and these ten loaves of bread to your brothers in camp. Hurry.
And these ten wheels of cheese — give them to the commander of their unit. Check on your brothers. See how they are. Bring back some token from them.
Saul and your brothers and all the men of Israel are in the Valley of Elah, fighting the Philistines."
David got up early, left the flock with a keeper, loaded up, and went, just as Jesse told him. He reached the camp circle just as the army was moving out to the battle line, shouting the war cry.
Israel and the Philistines lined up facing each other, rank to rank.
David dropped his supplies with the supply officer, ran to the front, and went looking for his brothers to see if they were all right.
He was still talking with them when the champion stepped out — Goliath of Gath — and shouted his usual taunts. David heard every word.
The Israelite soldiers, the moment they saw him, broke and ran. They were terrified.

They kept saying, "Have you seen this man who keeps coming out? He's here to humiliate Israel. The king has put a fortune on his head — and his daughter — and tax exemption for the man's whole family in Israel, for whoever kills him."

David turned to the men standing near him: "What does a man get for killing this Philistine and wiping the disgrace off Israel? Who does this uncircumcised Philistine think he is, mocking the armies of the living God?"
They told him the same thing again: "That's what the man who kills him gets."

Eliab, David's oldest brother, overheard him talking to the men, and his temper flared. "What are you even doing down here? Who is watching those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your arrogance, your reckless heart — you only came down to watch the battle."
David said, "What did I do now? It was just a question."
He turned away from him to someone else and asked the same thing. The men gave him the same answer.
Word of what David had said got around. It reached Saul, who sent for him.
David said to Saul, "Don't let anyone lose heart on account of this man. Your servant will go and fight him."
Saul said, "You cannot go up against this Philistine. You're a boy. He has been a warrior since his youth."
David answered, "Your servant tends his father's sheep. When a lion came — or a bear — and carried off a lamb from the flock,
I went after it, struck it down, and tore the lamb from its mouth. When it turned on me, I grabbed it by the beard, struck it, and killed it.
Lion and bear — your servant has killed them both. And this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, because he has mocked the armies of the living God.
The Lord who saved me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear — He will save me from the hand of this Philistine." Saul said to David, "Go. And may the Lord be with you."
Saul dressed David in his own gear — a bronze helmet on his head, a coat of armor on his body.
David strapped Saul's sword over the armor and tried to walk. He couldn't. He had never worn this. "I can't move in these," he said to Saul. "I'm not used to them." He stripped them off.

Then he took his staff in his hand, picked five smooth stones from the streambed, and dropped them into the shepherd's pouch he carried. With his sling in his hand, he walked out to meet the Philistine.
The Philistine came on, closing the distance, his shield-bearer in front of him.
He looked David over. And he despised him — just a boy, ruddy and handsome.
The Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?" And he cursed David by his gods.
"Come here," the Philistine said. "I'll feed your flesh to the birds of the air and the beasts of the field."
David said to the Philistine: "You come at me with sword and spear and javelin. I come at you in the name of the Lord of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel — the one you have mocked.

Today the Lord will hand you over to me. I will strike you down. I will take your head off your body. And today I will give the corpses of the Philistine army to the birds of the air and the wild beasts of the earth — so that all the earth will know there is a God in Israel.
And everyone gathered here will know that the Lord does not save by sword or spear. The battle belongs to the Lord. He will hand all of you over to us."
The Philistine started forward, moving in to meet him. David ran — sprinted toward the battle line, straight at the Philistine.
He reached into his pouch, pulled out a stone, slung it — and it struck the Philistine in the forehead. The stone sank in. He fell on his face to the ground.
So David beat the Philistine with a sling and a stone. He struck him down. He killed him. No sword in his hand.

David ran and stood over him, drew the Philistine's own sword from its sheath, and finished him — cut off his head with it.

When the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they broke and ran.

The men of Israel and Judah surged up, shouting, and chased the Philistines all the way to the entrance of the valley and the gates of Ekron. Philistine dead littered the road to Shaaraim, all the way to Gath and Ekron.
The Israelites came back from chasing the Philistines and looted their camp.
David took the Philistine's head and brought it to Jerusalem. The weapons he kept in his own tent.
When Saul had watched David go out against the Philistine, he had said to Abner, his commander, "Whose son is that boy, Abner?" Abner said, "On your life, O king — I have no idea."
The king said, "Find out whose son the young man is."
So when David came back from killing the Philistine, Abner brought him to Saul, the head of the Philistine still in his hand.
Saul said, "Whose son are you, young man?" David said, "The son of your servant Jesse, the Bethlehemite."

com.d:
# 1 Samuel 17: The Courage That Comes From Trust

David's confrontation with Goliath reveals that genuine courage is not the absence of fear, but faith in a God who is greater than every giant we face. This passage teaches us that the size of our problem matters far less than the size of our God.

When Israel's army stands paralyzed before Goliath, they measure the battle by human standards—weapons, armor, and physical stature. David, arriving with bread and cheese for his brothers, immediately sees what everyone else has missed: this isn't fundamentally a military problem. It's a spiritual one. Goliath blasphemes the living God, and that changes everything. David's famous declaration—"You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the Lord Almighty"—reveals that he has already won the battle in his heart before the first stone leaves his sling.

Notice how David's confidence isn't arrogance. He recounts his experience with the lion and bear, acknowledging that God protected him then. He draws courage from his history with God. This is profoundly practical: we grow bolder when we remember that God has been faithful before. David brings to the battlefield a testimony, not just a weapon.

For those of us facing our own giants—overwhelming circumstances, persistent fears, impossible relationships, health crises, or vocational challenges—this passage whispers an essential truth. Our giants are real, but they are not ultimate. The God who stands with us is infinitely more powerful than anything arrayed against us. Courage emerges not from denying difficulty but from trusting that we belong to a God who defeats what threatens us.

What giant in your life would shrink if you truly believed that God is on your side? Consider spending time today remembering how God has already proven faithful in your past, letting that history strengthen your faith for what you face now.
com.s:
The narrative of David's confrontation with Goliath stands as one of the most celebrated accounts in the Hebrew Bible, functioning within the larger Deuteronomistic History's presentation of David's rise to kingship. Composed likely during the late monarchic or exilic period, this chapter draws upon earlier traditions to establish David's credentials as YHWH's chosen successor to Saul. The account presents significant text-critical challenges, as the Septuagint preserves a considerably shorter version lacking verses 12–31, 41, 48b, 50, and 55–58, leading scholars to debate whether the Masoretic Text represents editorial expansion or the LXX reflects abbreviation of a longer Vorlage.

The Philistine champion is designated by the Hebrew term *gibbor* (גִּבּוֹר), denoting not merely physical prowess but warrior-elite status within ancient Near Eastern military culture. His height—six cubits and a span in the MT, four cubits and a span in the LXX and 4QSamᵃ—situates him within the Rephaim traditions of extraordinary warriors. The elaborate description of his bronze armor employs technical military vocabulary, emphasizing the seemingly insurmountable material advantage he possesses. Goliath's challenge invokes the ancient practice of representative combat (*ish-benayim*, literally "a man of the between"), whereby single combat could determine the outcome of broader conflicts.

David's response centers on the theological concept expressed through the phrase *ma'arkhot 'elohim chayyim* (מַעַרְכוֹת אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים)—"the ranks of the living God"—transforming the encounter from military contest to cosmic confrontation between YHWH and the false gods of Philistia. His rejection of Saul's armor in favor of shepherd's implements carries profound symbolic weight, demonstrating that Israel's security derives not from conventional military apparatus but from divine empowerment. The five smooth stones (*chalukey-'abanim chalukkot*) selected from the wadi serve as instruments of YHWH's deliverance.

Canonically, this narrative functions as legitimation theology, establishing David's worthiness through demonstrated courage, prophetic speech, and reliance upon YHWH—qualities conspicuously absent from Saul's paralyzed leadership. The tension between this account and the introduction of David in chapter 16 has generated extensive source-critical discussion regarding the composition history of the Samuel corpus and the integration of competing traditions about David's emergence into Israelite prominence.
com.p:
This beloved narrative unfolds approximately 1000 years before the incarnation of Christ, during the transitional period when Israel moved from the judges to the monarchy. David, likely a teenager, confronts Goliath in the Valley of Elah while Saul reigns as Israel's first king—a king already rejected by God for his disobedience. Within redemptive history, this passage stands in the Kingdom era, after the Exodus and conquest but before the Davidic covenant would be formally established in 2 Samuel 7. Here we witness the emergence of the man through whose lineage the Messiah would come.

The typological richness of this chapter resounds through the ages. Goliath stands as a type of Satan himself—the ancient serpent, the accuser, the one who defies the armies of the living God. For forty days this uncircumcised Philistine blasphemed and terrorized God's people, holding them in bondage through fear. The number forty echoes judgment and testing throughout Scripture. Israel's army, though numerous, stood paralyzed—a portrait of humanity's utter inability to defeat the enemy who held them captive through the fear of death.

Into this impossible situation steps David, the overlooked shepherd-king, bearing remarkable Christological significance. He comes not in Saul's armor—not in the strength of human institution or military might—but in the name of the Lord of hosts. He descends into the valley to face the giant alone while his brothers watch from the hillside, just as Christ descended from glory to confront the powers of darkness while humanity stood helpless. David's five smooth stones and single decisive blow foreshadow Christ's perfect victory accomplished through apparent weakness. The shepherd who protected his flock from lion and bear now delivers all Israel through his singular combat.

The beheading of Goliath with his own sword prophetically anticipates how Christ would defeat Satan using death itself as the instrument of destruction—the enemy's own weapon turned against him. What appeared to be Christ's defeat at Golgotha became the crushing of the serpent's head.

This victory remains partially fulfilled and partially future. Christ has dealt the decisive blow; the enemy is fatally wounded. Yet the church militant still faces Goliath's taunts in this present age. The complete manifestation of victory awaits the second advent when every enemy will be placed beneath the feet of great David's greater Son, and the reproach of God's people will be forever silenced.
